before: In South Carolina, you have three years from the crash date to file a personal-injury lawsuit under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530. Wrongful-death claims under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-51-10 also follow a three-year deadline from the date of death. Miss the date and the court will dismiss your case regardless of how clear the drunk driver's fault was. Narrow exceptions (minors, incapacitated plaintiffs, government defendants) can shift the timing.
after: In South Carolina, you have three years from the crash date to file a personal-injury lawsuit under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530. Wrongful-death claims (S.C. Code Ann. § 15-51-10) carry the same three years, running from the date of death under § 15-3-530(6), and are brought by the estate's personal representative (§ 15-51-20). Miss the date and the court will dismiss your case regardless of how clear the drunk driver's fault was. Narrow exceptions (minors, incapacitated plaintiffs, government defendants) can shift the timing; a claim against a government defendant generally has only two years under § 15-78-110.

before: Sometimes. South Carolina has no separate dram-shop statute, but bars and restaurants can be held civilly liable under common-law negligence for knowingly serving alcohol to a visibly intoxicated patron who then injures someone. These cases live or die on evidence — receipts, POS time stamps, surveillance video, witnesses to visible intoxication — and that evidence disappears fast without preservation letters in the first weeks.
after: Sometimes. South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but a bar or restaurant that knowingly serves an intoxicated patron violates S.C. Code Ann. §§ 61-4-580 and 61-6-2220, and courts treat that as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club, Inc., 332 S.C. 90 (1998); Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, Inc., 388 S.C. 407 (2010)). For claims arising after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 makes the establishment jointly and severally liable for 50% of your actual damages when the verdict also runs against a driver charged with DUI. These cases live or die on evidence — receipts, POS time stamps, surveillance video, witnesses to visible intoxication — and that evidence disappears fast without preservation letters in the first weeks.
